content: Since we have no metaprogramming in Tau Ceti, and arguably shouldn't (such things belong in Lean or Mathlib, but I'm happy to revisit this), for now we forbid meta import in Tau Ceti. This makes auditing slightly easier.
Perhaps not relevant to TauCeti for axiom reasons, but the bv_decide tactic does not work without a meta-import: #lean4 > error: Tactic `bv_decide` failed. Error: Invalid `meta` def @ 💬

I'm not sure if agents can come up with good metaprogramming abilities (my impression is they're too happy to repeat the same code a thousand times).

But if they're good enough to come up with good tactics by themselves, I don't see why not.

Big if though.

(More often than not, the purpose of metaprogramming is to avoid some repetition in code that cannot be eliminated otherwise. Which, thinking about it, if the reuse rubric reviewer flag code duplication, but the worker has no way to fix it because metaprogramming is disallowed, it would be stuck.)

I wouldn't be too concerned about auditing. If some agent find some shenanigan to sneak in a sorry or a proof of False with metaprogramming, that's a kernel bug and it better be fixed sooner than later.

user202729 said:

I wouldn't be too concerned about auditing. If some agent find some shenanigan to sneak in a sorry or a proof of False with metaprogramming, that's a kernel bug and it better be fixed sooner than later.

Tau Ceti may not be the best place to allow this to surface, it might cause days of token waste of other agents, following the same cheat pattern, producing massive invalid proofs, before a human tends to this. Forbidden it is a proper human attention investment to the infra, to save human attentions on watching out for the agents to turn rogue all of a sudden. The alternative would be some watcher agents burning tokens, but it is less reliable and a waste.

user202729 said:

if the reuse rubric reviewer flag code duplication, but the worker has no way to fix it because metaprogramming is disallowed, it would be stuck.

I had similar thought but with the idea of domain specific tactics. I tried to identify if some domain specific tactics will help improving proof quality and reuse, however repeatedly discussions with my agent revealed that those issues were better fixed with improvements to math APIs (or the better use of them), and they led to some of my refactor PRs , without needing new tactics at all (yet human attentions are scarce resource, and I didn't even have the time to do this in a weekly manner). Based on this experience, I believe an agent stuck by lack of meta programming is very unlikely, thus can't justify allowing it to use metaprogramming.

In the long run, I do hope agents will find useful patterns that should become tactics etc., but there would need infras to support agents to do it properly, yet I don't see anything like rubrics for that in sight. Right now such cases could only surface with human attention, human discussions on the design etc. and such effort would likely land them in mathlib or lean anyway.
